title: Metabolic reconfiguration through SGLT2 inhibition improves metabolic waste excretion
projectDescription: Dapagliflozin is a member of a new class of medication called gliflozins indicated for the treatment of diabetes and has recently been also approved for the treatment of kidney and heart diseases. Gliflozins lower blood glucose levels by inhibition of the sodium glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2), which is predominantly expressed in the S1 segment of renal proximal tubules and responsible for >90% of renal glucose reabsorption. Renal and cardio protection by gliflozins cannot be solely explained by blood glucose lowering. To gain further mechanistic insights, we determined the metabolomic and proteomic signature of dapagliflozin in a murine model of diabetes. Male C57BL/6 non-diabetic wildtype and littermate Ins2 (Akita) diabetic mice, both fed a Western diet for 5 weeks, were given dapagliflozin (10 mg/kg diet) or vehicle for one week (4 groups, N=8/group). Blood and urine glucose levels confirmed the expected treatment response. We analyzed metabolome, proteome and phosphoproteome for a range of tissues (kidney, liver, heart, smooth muscle, white adipose tissue) and body fluids (serum, urine, erythrocytes), and extended the analysis to the gut metaproteome.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Protein extraction. Tissue pieces (20-40 mg) and gut bacteria were homogenized in 300 µl extraction buffer at 4°C by bead-beating in a bullet blender (Storm) for 3 min with amplitude 8 (2 steel beads per sample). Proteins were extracted in a buffer containing 6M guanidinium hydochloride, 10 mM HEPES (pH8.5), 5 mM TCEP, 10 mM chloroacetamide, supplemented with protease inhibitors (Complete, Roche), phosphatase inhibitors (PHosStop, Roche) and benzonase (200 U/ml). After boiling (10 min, 95°C) protein concentrations were determined by BCA assay. Samples were diluted to 1M guanidinum hydrochloride and proteins were digested with trypsin at 37°C overnight at an enzyme to protein ratio of 1:50. Digestion was stopped by adding TFA to a final concentration of 1%. Peptides were desalted by reverse phase 5xC18 disks StageTipping. Peptides were dried down and reconstituted in 100 mM TEAB (pH8.5). Peptide concentrations were determined by NanoDrop.  TMT labeling. Peptides were labeled with TMTproTM 16-plex according to manufacturer´s instructions allowing direct comparisons between DAPA (n=8) and CTRL (n=8) per organ (kidney, liver, heart, muscle, white adipose tissue, gut microbiome) separately for each mouse strain (wt, Akita). In total, 12 TMTproTM 16-plex labeling reactions were performed.  Phosphopeptide enrichment. TMT labeled peptides (120-200 µg) were desalted on C18 SepPak columns. Dried down peptides were reconstituted in loading buffer (80% acetonitrile, 1M glycolic acid, and 5% TFA). To each sample 500 µg equilibrated MagReSyn® Ti-IMAC magnetic beads (ReSyn Biosciences) were added and incubated while shaking for 20 min. Beads were separated on a magnetic stand for 30s. Phosphopeptides were washed for two min loading buffer, followed by two washes in 80% acetonitrile, 1% TFA, and a final wash with 10% acetonitrile, 0.2% TFA. Enriched phosphopeptides were eluted in 3 rounds with 80 µl 1% ammonia for 20 min and were acidified with TFA. After drying down peptides were loaded and desalted on C18 Stage Tips. Reverse phase high pH peptide fractionation. TMT-labeled peptides for proteome and phosphoproteome analysis were dried down, desalted on C18 Stage Tips and stepwise eluted in 25 mM ammonium formate (pH10) with increasing concentrations of acetonitrile (10%, 12.5%, 15%, 17.5%, 20%, 22.5%, 25%, 50%) resulting in eight fractions per sample.  Mass spectrometry measurements. Tryptic peptides in 0.1% formic acid were analyzed on an UltiMate3000 RSLC system (Thermo Fisher Scientific) coupled to an Exploris 480 mass spectromter including FAIMS pro interface (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Peptides were separated on a two-column set-up with a trap column (Acclaim™ PepMap™ 100 C18, 3µm particle size, 2 cm x 75 µm, ThermoFisher Scientific) at a flowrate of 5 µl/min and an analytical column (Aurora 25 cm x 75 µm, IonOpticks) at a flowrate of 400 nl/min using a 150 min gradient with mobile phase A as 0.1% formic acid in LC-MS-grade water and mobile phase B as 0.1% formic acid in LC-MS-grade acetonitrile. The peptide gradient was run for 5 min at 2% B, followed by a linear gradient to 30% B over 120 min, at 126 min to switched 90% B and finished with a column equilibration step from 136 -150 min at 2% B. All mass spectrometry measurements were recorded in data-dependent mode in positive polarity with 3 FAIMS CV voltages: for proteome -40, -55, -70 and for phosphoproteome -40, -60, -80. Cycle times were 1s for each CV voltage. MS1 spectra were recorded in profile mode at 120K resolution within a scan range of 350-1350 m/z, with normalized AGC target of 300%, RF lens of 40%, included charge states of 2-6, minimal intensity of 5x104 and auto maximum injection time. MS2 spectra were recorded in centroid mode at 45K with a normalized HCD collision energy of 32% (35% for phosphoproteome), an isolation window of 0.7 m/z, a normalized AGC target of 75%, a fixed first mass at 110 m/z and auto maximum injection time.
dataProcessingProtocol: All RAW files were analyzed by Proteome Discoverer v2.4. Proteome and phosphoproteome was analyzed separately with one analysis per organ combining wt and Akita. In total 10 Proteome Discoverer searches for organs were performed, 5 for proteome (kidney, liver heart, muscle, fat) and 5 for phosphoproteome (kidney, liver heart, muscle, fat), with SeQuest as search engine and a Mus musculus proteome database downloaded from UniProt. For Metaproteome analysis RAW files were analyzed separately for wt and Akita with SeQuest as search engine. A project-specific database for the gut microbiome constructed from metagenomics as well as a murine database (same as for Proteome and Phosphoproteome analysis) were used. Downstream analyses were performed in R. Statistical analysis was performed with the Limma package.
